Newborn Care

Hepatitis C and breastfeeding: milk, blood exposure and follow-up

Updated: October 19, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Hepatitis C virus (HCV) mainly spreads through infected blood. There is no documented evidence that breastfeeding itself transmits HCV, so an HCV diagnosis alone does not mean a baby must stop receiving breast milk. Nipple injury, a possible blood exposure, other infections and the exact medicines being used can change the plan. Parent and infant follow-up remain important even when feeding is going well.

Milk transmission is different from infection during pregnancy or birth

HCV causes a liver infection and can be passed through blood, sometimes in amounts too small to see. A baby can acquire HCV during pregnancy or delivery; that is different from infection through breast milk. Breastfeeding has not been shown to increase HCV transmission, and expressed milk is not automatically unsafe because the parent has HCV.

Laboratory findings about milk affecting the virus do not guarantee that every possible exposure is harmless. In particular, milk potentially contaminated with blood from a damaged nipple needs a different approach. If there is HIV coinfection or another medical issue, ask the specialist team for an individual feeding plan rather than applying HCV-only advice.

Cracked, damaged or bleeding nipples need a temporary plan

If a nipple or the surrounding areola is cracked, damaged or bleeding, temporarily pause feeding from the injured area and contact a skilled feeding professional or clinician. HCV can spread through blood, and the precise risk in this situation is not well established. Do not offer expressed milk that may contain blood as an alternative to direct feeding.

CDC advises expressing and discarding milk while the nipples heal to help maintain production. Obtain advice on comfortable expression, which milk can be used and when direct feeding can resume; the usual aim is to resume once the injury has healed. Do not boil milk at home or assume that a bottle removes the blood-exposure concern.

Keep the baby fed and address the cause of injury

A temporary feeding plan may include pasteurized donor human milk from an appropriate service or suitable infant formula, with preparation instructions for the baby's age and health. Ask the team what is available and how much support you need. Avoid informal promises that donated milk is screened or safe, and never use homemade or over-diluted formula.

Have attachment, positioning and pump fit assessed. Too much suction or an uncomfortable flange can worsen injury; expression should not mean pushing through pain. Get help for persistent pain, skin damage or difficulty transferring milk. The aim is to protect the baby, your comfort and milk production without unnecessary permanent weaning or blame.

Everyday closeness and household blood precautions

HCV does not spread through ordinary hugging, kissing, holding hands, sharing food or drink, coughing or sneezing. An infected caregiver does not need to withdraw from everyday affection. Focus precautions on blood exposure, including blood contacting broken skin, an eye or the mouth, rather than treating the person or all household belongings as contaminated.

Do not share razors, toothbrushes, nail clippers or other items that may have blood on them. Keep sharps and personal care equipment away from children. Cover cuts with a suitable dressing, and prevent a bleeding wound from contacting the baby. If a mouth sore is bleeding, avoid exposing the baby to that blood and seek advice; ordinary kissing without blood is not an HCV transmission route.

Care for wounds and clean blood safely

For a small cut, control the bleeding, clean it and apply an appropriate plaster or dressing. Seek care for a deep wound, uncontrolled bleeding, a retained object or signs of infection. A caregiver with a covered injury does not automatically have to stop caring for the baby; arrange help if the wound cannot be safely covered or blood could reach the child.

Use gloves when handling blood or blood-stained dressings, keep the baby away from a spill, and clean the area promptly with products suitable for the surface, following their label. Dispose of contaminated materials securely and keep them out of children's reach; wash hands afterwards. Surface disinfectants belong on suitable surfaces, not on the baby's skin, mouth or feeding equipment contrary to its instructions.

If the baby or a caregiver has contact with blood

Wash exposed skin or a cut with soap and water; flush a splash to the mouth or nose with water and an eye with clean water or saline. Do not put household disinfectant, alcohol or an 'antiviral' product on the baby to try to prevent infection. A splash to the eyes or mouth, blood on broken skin, or a sharps injury needs immediate clinical advice and an exposure-specific plan.

Tell the team when it happened, how contact occurred and what is known about the source infection. HCV does not have a routinely recommended antiviral post-exposure prevention course, but testing and treatment if infection develops are available. HIV and hepatitis B have different prevention options that can be time-sensitive. Do not wait for symptoms, self-prescribe antivirals or assume that the routine perinatal infant test schedule covers a new blood exposure.

Antibody testing and HCV RNA answer different questions

An HCV antibody test indicates possible previous or current infection; a positive result alone does not establish that the virus is still present. A nucleic acid test (NAT), often using PCR, looks for HCV RNA and helps identify current infection. HCV is an RNA virus; an antibody test is not the same thing as an RNA PCR test.

A negative antibody result soon after exposure may be too early to exclude infection. A clinician may use RNA testing and arrange follow-up according to the timing, symptoms and immune status. Ask what each result means and which test is next. Neither fatigue nor a symptom-free appearance can establish someone's HCV status.

Testing the parent and reassessing after delivery

HCV often causes no symptoms. Testing is relevant after a possible blood exposure, with ongoing risks such as shared injecting equipment, or when a clinician identifies another indication. CDC also recommends screening during each pregnancy and at least once for adults in most settings; local programmes differ. Fever, tiredness, abdominal discomfort or concentration problems can have many causes and should not be used to diagnose HCV.

If HCV was present in pregnancy, arrange an HCV RNA reassessment after delivery. Levels can fall, remain detectable or rise again, and some people clear infection without treatment. A percentage from one small postpartum study is not your personal chance of clearance. Follow-up RNA results and clinical assessment, rather than waiting or assuming recovery, guide the treatment discussion.

Testing a baby exposed during pregnancy or birth

Arrange the baby's testing plan with the paediatric team even if the baby seems well. Current CDC guidance recommends an HCV RNA NAT at two to six months for perinatally exposed infants. An antibody test before eighteen months can detect antibodies transferred from the birth parent, so it cannot substitute for the appropriate early RNA test.

Under CDC guidance, an infant with detectable RNA needs paediatric HCV expertise; an undetectable RNA result at or after two months usually needs no further HCV follow-up unless clinically warranted. If not previously tested, children aged seven to seventeen months need an RNA NAT, while those eighteen months or older have antibody testing with reflex RNA if reactive. Follow the child's local specialist pathway, which may differ, and seek a new assessment for a later exposure or illness.

A positive result and treatment for a child

A positive infant result is not a reason to blame feeding or assume permanent liver damage. The specialist confirms the infection, monitors the child and considers other health needs. Some children clear HCV spontaneously, but that possibility does not remove the need for follow-up.

Approved direct-acting antivirals can treat HCV from age three years in appropriate children. The clinician checks current infection again and selects a product and formulation for age, weight, liver health and other factors. Testing should happen before treatment age; there is no reason to wait until the third birthday to identify an exposed infant or arrange care.

HCV treatment while breastfeeding requires drug-specific advice

Modern oral direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) cure most people, often with an eight- to twelve-week course, but the regimen and follow-up depend on the individual. Discuss liver health, other medicines, hepatitis B status, future pregnancy plans and the baby's age and health with the prescriber. Do not start, stop or change treatment or stop breastfeeding solely on the basis of a general article.

Newer human milk measurements for sofosbuvir/velpatasvir found low estimated infant exposure in a very small study. July 2026 LactMed assessments do not regard the listed sofosbuvir- or velpatasvir-containing combinations alone as a reason to discontinue breastfeeding, but infant outcome data remain limited. Existing product information is more cautious and requires weighing benefits and risks. Neither 'all DAAs are safe' nor 'all treatment must wait until weaning' is a reliable rule; the exact combination, any additional drug and the infant's circumstances need specialist review. Pregnancy evidence is a separate question, not proof of lactation safety.

Make follow-up and feeding support practical

Keep the parent's RNA results, medicine list, nipple-healing plan and infant testing appointment together. Ask whom to contact if a nipple bleeds again, expression hurts, a medicine changes or a result is delayed. An app or written note can help with organisation, but cannot determine infection status or whether a sample is contaminated with blood.

Seek prompt clinical advice for jaundice, worsening illness, a painful inflamed breast with fever, or problems feeding the baby. A baby with breathing difficulty, abnormal blue or grey colour, difficulty waking or a seizure needs emergency care; fever of 38°C or more in a baby under three months needs immediate medical assessment. Do not delay care to complete a feed or wait for an HCV test. These signs do not by themselves diagnose hepatitis C.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask for a written nipple-injury feeding plan and infant testing dates; seek feeding help early if pain, cracking or bleeding develops.

Bring current RNA results and all medicines to the specialist; ask about treatment during breastfeeding for your exact regimen and baby's circumstances.

After a blood exposure, use appropriate first aid and seek immediate clinical advice; do not apply disinfectants or antiviral products to the baby or wait for symptoms.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help keep feeding observations, symptoms, test dates and questions for the team together. It cannot diagnose HCV, interpret RNA or antibody results, assess blood-contaminated milk or confirm that a medicine is suitable. Clinical exposure and urgent-care advice takes priority over app records.

When to seek help

Pause feeding from cracked or bleeding nipples and get a temporary feeding plan; do not offer milk that may contain blood. Blood contact with an eye, mouth, broken skin or a sharps injury needs immediate clinical advice. Do not use household disinfectant or an antiviral product on the baby, self-prescribe antivirals or alter prescribed treatment. Seek emergency care for a baby with breathing difficulty, blue or grey colour, difficulty waking or a seizure, and immediate assessment for fever of 38°C or more under three months. Do not wait for an HCV result or finish a feed before getting help.

Evidence notes updated: October 19, 2026

Key takeaways

  • HCV mainly spreads through blood; breastfeeding itself has no documented transmission risk.
  • Cracked, damaged or bleeding nipples need a temporary feeding and expression plan, with help to heal the injury.
  • Ordinary affection does not spread HCV; focus household precautions on blood and shared sharp or personal care items.
  • RNA and antibody tests differ; arrange early perinatal infant testing and postpartum parent follow-up.
  • Treatment and feeding decisions must consider the exact medicine and infant, rather than a blanket safety or weaning rule.

Frequently asked questions

Can hepatitis C pass through breast milk?

There is no documented evidence that breastfeeding transmits HCV. Blood exposure from nipple injury is a separate concern, as are infection acquired during pregnancy or delivery and medicine-specific feeding advice.

Can a parent with hepatitis C breastfeed or express milk?

Usually yes when nipples are healthy and there is no other contraindication. Do not assume milk laboratory findings guarantee safety with blood contamination. Discuss any medicine, HIV coinfection or other medical issue with the care team.

What should I do if a nipple is cracked or bleeding?

Temporarily pause feeding from the injured area and do not give milk that may contain blood. Ask for feeding support; CDC advises expressing and discarding while nipples heal, with donor milk or formula support when needed. Plan a return once healed rather than stopping permanently without advice.

When should an exposed baby be tested?

For exposure during pregnancy or birth, current CDC guidance recommends an HCV RNA NAT at two to six months. Catch-up testing depends on age. Maternal antibodies can persist until eighteen months, so an early antibody test is not an equivalent substitute. A new blood exposure needs its own immediate assessment.

Does a positive antibody test mean active hepatitis C?

Not necessarily. Antibodies can remain after an infection has cleared. RNA testing identifies current infection; recent exposure can also require RNA testing despite a negative antibody result. Ask your clinician to interpret the combination and timing.

Should we avoid holding or kissing the baby?

HCV is not spread by ordinary hugging, kissing or holding hands. Cover wounds, avoid blood contact and do not share items that can carry blood. A bleeding wound or mouth sore needs specific precautions rather than general isolation.

Must HCV treatment wait until breastfeeding ends?

Not automatically. Recent drug-specific milk data are reassuring about low exposure for some combinations, but infant evidence is limited and product information remains cautious. A specialist should weigh the exact regimen, your need for treatment and the baby's health; do not change medicines or feeding on your own.

Will the baby need treatment immediately after a positive test?

The paediatric specialist arranges confirmation and monitoring. Some infections clear, while approved DAA treatment is available from age three in suitable children. Early testing and follow-up are still important even though medicines are not routinely started in infancy.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
